messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Nguyen was thirty-three years old, a physical therapist at an outpatient clinic in the East Bay, and until eighteen months ago he had never questioned the dependability of his own body. That changed on a Tuesday morning in December, when a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at an intersection he had driven through every workday for five years. The impact pushed the driver’s side door into his hip and ribs; he remembers the sound of metal crumpling and the smell of leaking coolant more clearly than he remembers the pain. He was cut out of the car by firefighters, spent three days in the hospital with a fractured pelvis and two cracked ribs, and was discharged with a clean bill of health and a prescription for physical therapy—his own profession’s domain. He healed. The X-rays cleared. But something inside him never did.

In the weeks after the accident, Minh began waking in the dark with his heart racing, the screech of twisting steel still ringing in his ears. He would lie motionless, listening to his wife’s breathing beside him, afraid that if he moved he would hear his own bones grind. The thoughts arrived unbidden during the day too: a flash of windshield glass, the truck’s grille filling his vision, the certainty that he was about to die. He tried to push them away, but they came back, and he started to believe that his body had been permanently hollowed out by the crash—that whatever damage the doctors had missed was still there, dormant, waiting to betray him. He no longer trusted his own strength. The idea that he could be harmed by someone else, anyone else, began to feel like a law of the world rather than a possibility.

At the clinic, Minh’s work became a minefield. A patient dropping a five-pound weight against the floor made him jump so hard he nearly dropped the treatment table. The noise—sharp, sudden, metallic—sent a jolt through him that took minutes to settle. He began scanning every room he entered: the gym floor, the supply closet, the breakroom. He noticed the scissors on the desk, the crutch tips that could be used as a blunt object, the metal base of the IV stand. He didn’t think these things would be used against him, exactly—he just saw them now, as if the world had been seeded with threats he had been blind to before. Concentration became elusive. While guiding a patient through a hamstring stretch, his mind would drift into rehearsals: What if a car crashes through the front wall? What if a patient suddenly becomes violent? He would mentally walk through worst-case scenarios, step by step, telling himself that if he rehearsed them enough he would be ready. But he never felt ready.

At home, he developed rituals he kept private from his wife, Lan. He started cleaning the kitchen counters three times before he could sit down to eat, rearranging the spice jars until the labels all faced forward. He knew it was irrational, but the act of ordering a small space quieted something in his chest. He checked the locks on the doors twice before bed, and once again after he lay down. Lan noticed the extra tension in his shoulders, his reluctance to drive them anywhere on weekends. She asked if he was okay. He said he was fine, but he avoided her eyes. He stopped driving the route where the accident happened, always taking the longer way through side streets, scanning every intersection for the shape of a truck.

The consequences crept into his work life quietly. A supervisor mentioned that his documentation had been late. He forgot a patient’s exercise progression in the middle of a session, froze for a moment, then covered with a joke that didn’t land. He began staying late to clean the treatment tables and organize the shelves, telling himself it was for infection control. In truth, it was the only time he felt a flicker of calm.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a morning three weeks ago. He had woken from a nightmare—the same one, the crash—and found himself standing in the bathroom, scrubbing the sink with a toothbrush at four in the morning. Lan was in the doorway, saying his name softly. He couldn’t stop shaking. He realized then that he had not felt safe in his own body, in his own home, in over a year. He didn’t know if therapy could fix what was broken, but he was terrified that if he didn’t try, he would spend the rest of his life cleaning things that were already clean and rehearsing disasters that never came. He wanted to believe that his body could be trusted again, and that the world was not, in fact, a place where harm waited around every corner.
